rendered:
The document does not report any results for a D-HGNR-based probe on the clinical sepsis serum samples. Those samples were tested only with the L-configured probe.

**Why the D probe was dropped:** The authors compared the L- and D-HGNR probes early on. The CD signals had opposite signs, but the response sizes were closely comparable[1], so the authors chose BA@L-HGNRs were employed as the probe for subsequent work.[2]

**Where the D probe does appear:** It was used only to check the discrimination of the bacterial strains: The BA@D-HGNRs probe with the opposite spatial configuration also effectively validates this phenomenon (Fig.S16).[3]

**The clinical sepsis test (L probe only):** Serum came from septic patients with confirmed E. coli infection, septic patients with confirmed E. faecium infection, and healthy volunteers. The LDA plot showed well-resolved, non-overlapping clusters for the three tested serum groups, demonstrating the great potential of the BA@L-HGNRs probe for accurate bacterial discrimination in serum samples from septic patients[4] (see Fig. 5[5], panel c).

So the document has no data on how a D-HGNR-based probe would perform on clinical sepsis serum.
